To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the generalization properties of stochastic optimization algorithms are intimately related to their sample complexity, (2) full-batch optimization algorithms are fundamentally limited in terms of their sample complexity, and (3) the generalization gap of stochastic optimization algorithms is related to the number of iterations, rather than the number of iterations per epoch, as previously believed
(a) full-batch methods do not generalize as well as stochastic methods (b) full-batch optimization is not a good proxy for stochastic optimization.

(a) the sample complexity of full-batch methods is $\Omega(d^2/\epsilon^4) \gg 1/\epsilon^3$ for $d$-dimensional data, while (b) stochastic algorithms are $\Theta(1/\epsilon)$-optimal, and (c) the iteration complexity of full-bath methods is $\Omega(1)$, while (d) stochastic algorithms are $O(1)$-optimal.

a fundamental question in optimization: can we go faster by using more data? Our answer is no, at least in the case of full-batch methods.

, in order to generalize, full-batch algorithms must be allowed to use a sample size that depends on the problem's dimension, and that this is a fundamental limitation.
